title: Task 4 - Git and GitHub Repository Initialization
prereq: Git installed (`git --version`). Nothing else needs to be running.
The GitHub step reads the public repository over the internet (read-only, no login). If you are offline, open https://github.com/KemNxts/hotel-room-booking-cicd in a browser instead.
Open PowerShell in the project folder. These commands only read the repository; none of them changes it.

recovery.fix: Install Git for Windows or open the 'Git Bash' / VS Code terminal where it is on the PATH.
You are in the wrong folder. `cd D:\DevOPS\CICD_FOR_HOTEL_ROOM_BOOKING`.

recovery.symptom: Different branch name / commit IDs than in the video
recovery.fix: Normal: history moves on. Explain the idea (branches, tags, remote) with what your screen shows. `git switch develop` is safe if there is nothing uncommitted (`git status` first).

recovery.symptom: GitHub request fails (rate limit or offline)
recovery.fix: Open the repository page in a browser: it shows 19 branches and the tags v1.0.0 and v1.1.0.

extra.what: The whole history as a graph, all branches

extraQuestions.q: The project document says it was not pushed to GitHub. Is that still true?
extraQuestions.a: No. That note in docs/04-git-workflow.md was written before the push and is out of date. The repository was pushed on 12 October 2026 (all branches and both tags) and the live check in this video confirms it: public repository, 19 branches, tags v1.0.0 and v1.1.0. What still does not exist on GitHub are issues and pull requests; the PR texts are prepared in docs/pull-requests/.

steps.title: The repository and its key files
steps.say: This is Task 4, Git and GitHub repository initialization. A repository is the project folder plus its complete history, stored in a hidden dot git folder. Here I list the Git related items in the project root: the dot git folder, the dot github folder, dot gitattributes, dot gitignore, CONTRIBUTING, README and a VERSION file. Each one has a purpose, and I will open them.
steps.tell: The repository contains the standard project files that every team repository should have.

steps.title: README: the front page
steps.say: The README is the front page of the project. It says what the project is, what the features are, and links to the documentation. Anyone who opens the repository on GitHub reads this first. It also contains the commands to run and test the application.
steps.expect: Project title, a one paragraph description, the current release in the VERSION file, and pointers to the project report and the 15-task checklist.
steps.tell: The README explains the project and where to find everything.

steps.title: .gitignore: what Git must not store
steps.say: The dot gitignore file lists files that Git must never store: the virtual environment, the database, test reports, environment files with passwords, and certificates. Here are the real rules. Then I ask Git itself, with check ignore, why three files are ignored. It names the rule and the line number. That is how secrets like the Jenkins password file stay out of the repository.
steps.expect: The list of ignore patterns, then three lines of the form '.gitignore:27:.env   deploy/jenkins/.env', showing the rule that ignores each file.
steps.tell: Passwords, databases and virtual environments are excluded from the repository by rule.

steps.title: .gitattributes: line endings
steps.say: The dot gitattributes file tells Git how to treat text files. Windows uses a different line ending than Linux. The first rule stores everything with Linux line endings in the repository. That matters because our Dockerfiles, Ansible files and scripts run inside Linux containers, and Windows line endings would break them.
steps.expect: '* text=auto eol=lf' stores LF line endings; .bat and .ps1 keep CRLF; images are marked binary.
steps.tell: Line endings are fixed by rule so files written on Windows still work inside Linux containers.

steps.title: CONTRIBUTING: the team rules
steps.say: CONTRIBUTING documents the team conventions. Main holds released code. Develop is where features meet and are tested together. Every change is made on its own feature branch, cut from develop. Branch names are lowercase with hyphens, and experiment branches are never merged. Writing the rules down means everyone works the same way.
steps.expect: A table of branches (main, develop, feature/*) with their purpose and who merges into them, followed by the naming rules.
steps.tell: The branching rules and commit conventions are documented in CONTRIBUTING.

steps.title: Issue templates
steps.say: These are the issue templates in the dot github folder. A bug report template and a feature request template give every issue the same structure: what happened, what was expected, and acceptance criteria. GitHub shows them automatically when someone clicks New issue.
steps.expect: Three template files, then the content of the feature request template.
steps.tell: Templates for issues and pull requests are ready so everyone reports in the same format.

steps.title: Pull request template and review checklist
steps.say: This is the pull request template. When a developer opens a pull request, GitHub pre fills this text. It asks what the change does and how it was tested, and gives an author checklist: branch name, commit message, linter clean, tests passing, Jenkins green and no secrets. A reviewer has a second checklist below. This is what supports code review.
steps.expect: Sections: What does this PR do, How was it tested, and the author checklist with seven boxes.
steps.tell: Every change goes through a checklist before it is merged.

steps.title: Branches that exist today
steps.say: Now the real repository. Git status shows the current branch and whether anything is changed. A branch is a separate line of development. Below is the list of all local branches: main for releases, develop for integration, many feature branches, fix branches, and two experiment branches. The star marks the branch I am on now.
steps.expect: The current branch with a star, then 20 local branches: main, develop, feature/*, fix/*, experiment/*, docs/*. Untracked files in the demonstrations folder are this recording work.
steps.tell: Every feature has its own branch; main and develop are the long-lived ones.

steps.title: History as a graph
steps.say: The log graph shows the history. Each line is a commit, a saved snapshot with a message. The lines with a slash show a feature branch splitting from develop and merging back. The names in brackets are branches. Each feature, such as nights column or ansible rollback, is visible as a unit because we merged with no fast forward.
steps.expect: A graph of commits; merge commits named 'Merge branch feature/... into develop', each with the feature's own commits beside it.
steps.tell: The history shows each feature as its own branch merged into develop.

steps.title: Tags and the remote
steps.say: A tag is a permanent label on one commit, used for releases. We have version 1.0.0 and 1.1.0. A branch moves forward as you commit, a tag stays put. A remote is another copy of the repository on a server. Ours is called origin and points to GitHub. The address contains no password.
steps.expect: Two tags with their messages, and origin fetch/push URLs of the public GitHub repository.
steps.tell: Releases are tagged and the remote copy lives on GitHub.

steps.title: Local repository versus the GitHub repository
steps.say: Local and remote are different things. My local repository is on this laptop. The remote is on GitHub. So I ask GitHub directly. It confirms a public repository, with nineteen branches and both release tags, and the develop branch is at the same commit locally and on GitHub. Issues and pull requests do not exist yet, only their templates and prepared texts.
steps.cmd: $u = 'https://api.github.com/repos/KemNxts/hotel-room-booking-cicd'; $r = Invoke-RestMethod $u; "$($r.full_name)  public=$(-not $r.private)  default=$($r.default_branch)"; "branches on GitHub: $((Invoke-RestMethod "$u/branches?per_page=100").Count)"; 'tags on GitHub: ' + ((Invoke-RestMethod "$u/tags").name -join ', '); git log --oneline -1 develop; git log --oneline -1 origin/develop
steps.expect: KemNxts/hotel-room-booking-cicd public=True default=main; 19 branches; tags v1.1.0, v1.0.0; the same commit id for develop and origin/develop.
steps.tell: The project is on GitHub with all branches and tags; the remaining GitHub work is issues and pull requests.

steps.title: Anatomy of one commit
steps.say: Finally, one commit in detail. It has an identifier, an author, a date and a message that follows our convention: type, colon, short description. Here feat means a new feature. The statistics show exactly which files changed, here the my bookings template and a test. Small, focused commits make review and rollback easy.
steps.expect: Commit 2d67e39 'feat: show number of nights in the My bookings list' changing a template and a test file (10 insertions, 1 deletion).
steps.tell: A commit is a small, labelled snapshot that shows exactly what changed and why.
